Infiniti’s QX80 Becomes a Premium Pickup in New Renderings
7 photos
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik
Are you one of those people who believes that the car world today should offer a plethora of premium pickups? If you said yes, then chances are you will like the project pictured below, which a workhorse version of the Infiniti QX80 .
Mind you, the word “pictured” does not really do justice to this thing, because “rendered” would suit it much better. That’s because this thing does not exist in the real world, as you already know, and it is the work of @kelsonik. The pixel master shared these digital illustration on his social media channels earlier in the week, sketching it out from a couple of angles, and directly comparing it to the SUV.
The front fascia is pretty much the same, save for the revised main clusters, which look different. The DRLs, the imposing grille, and even the bumper carries over, though the lower part of the latter component has been virtually altered. The hood and the front fenders carry over, and this includes the trim on the latter, but there are some significant changes on the sides that deserve their own paragraph.
For one, the wheel arch trim is now painted black, and it is much more pronounced on this rendered Infiniti QX80 Pickup. The side steps are also new, and the seem to have been digitally crafted from steel. The windows and the front doors are pretty much the same as before, though the rear doors now end abruptly right in front of the rear bed. The rear three-quarter panels are thus new as well, and the roofline is obviously much shorter.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik At the rear, we can see that the taillights have also been modified, and they do not extend into the new tailgate that opens up into a generous cargo area. Infiniti’s name decorates the drop-down tailgate. The bumper is exclusive to this model, and so are the wheels, which are not only new, but they have been shod in very fat tires for enhanced traction off the beaten path.
We can also see that this rendered Infiniti QX80 Pickup features a small opening in the rear windscreen, and that it rides a bit higher off the ground, so the suspension has also been modified during the pixel-altering process. The vehicle features a tan-line paint finish, has black wheels, several other black elements on the outside, a visible tailpipe below the rear bumper, and tinted rear windows, among other things.
Should Infiniti go ahead and launch its own workhorse? And would the QX80 be a good starting point? That’s for you to decide, though before inviting you to drop a few lines in the comments box at the bottom of the page, we will remind you that the third generation model has been around for a little over two years. It comes to life in Japan, at the Nissan Shatai Kyushu Plant in Kanda, and it shares its nuts and bolts with the Y63 Nissan Patrol / Armada.
The SUV is 211.2 inches (5,364 mm) long, 83.3 inches (2,116 mm) wide, and 76.6 inches (1,946 mm) tall, and the space between the axles measures 121 inches (3,073 mm). Therefore, a hypothetical pickup version based on this model would be smaller than the Ford Ranger, as this one has a 128.7 inches (3,270 mm) wheelbase, and measures up to 211.4 inches (5,370 mm) in length, with the sporty Raptor being slightly longer.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik The QX80 is Infiniti’s flagship SUV, and its lineup also includes the smaller QX60 and the QX65 in our market. The latter has an MSRP of $53,990 for the 2027 model year, and the former kicks off at $57,290, the company’s official US website reveals.
As for the 2027 Infiniti QX80 , you will have to fork out at least $88,590 for the base model, excluding destination, options, and dealer fees. The entry-level Pure 4WD is followed by the Luxe 4WD, which has an MSRP of $95,170 attached to it for the 2027 model year. The Sport 4WD kicks off at $103,285, and for the top-of-the-line grade, which is called the Autograph 4WD, you will have to cough out a minimum of $113,685.
All versions of the SUV pack the same engine, which is a V6 with twin turbocharging, and a 3.5-liter displacement. The mill is officially rated at 450 horsepower (456 ps/331 kW) at 5,600 rpm and 516 pound-feet (700 Nm) of torque at 3,600 rpm, working in concert with a nine-speed automatic transmission that channels everything to the four-wheel drive system, regardless of the selected trim level.
Infiniti has not revealed the 0-60 mph (0-97 kph) time, but independent testing shows from 5.5 to over 6 seconds, depending on the trim level and equipment, and the top speed is 123 mph (198 kph).
Now, do you think Infiniti should launch a premium pickup? And would the QX80 be a good foundation stone? Let’s not forget that others failed (ahem, Mercedes X-Class) in this game. View this post on Instagram A post shared by CAR DESIGN | RENDERINGS (@kelsonik)

1966 Chevy Impala Sitting on Private Property Begs for Restoration With a Big Block on the Outside
29 photos
Photo: eBay seller tolu-988
A 1966 Chevrolet Impala is certainly worth checking out if you are in the market for a restoration project, and this specimen is trying to convince the audience with a big-block engine. However, you don’t need to be a diehard restoration guy to figure out the obvious.
This isn’t an easy project, and whoever buys the car will have to do extensive work in all key areas, including the engine.
The big block I told you about is on the outside, as it has already been removed from the car, probably to be rebuilt. It hasn’t been rebuilt, so the only thing the current owner did was to remove the engine, and that’s all.
Photo: eBay seller tolu-988 1966 was such a big year for the Impala. America’s best-selling car was now all about big blocks, and the Super Sport was more powerful than ever.
This was the second year of a new generation that started in 1965 and whose sales went through the roof. The 1965 Impala was the first car in the United States to sell more than 1 million units in one year, and Chevrolet hoped the 1966 model year would do the same.
However, some of the changes the GM brand operated in the Impala lineup prevented the Impala from reaching the same numbers, despite the full-size series still selling like hotcakes. The Caprice was now a stand-alone series - no longer being part of the Impala lineup - so on paper, the Impala looked less successful - it wasn’t.
Chevrolet ended the year with over 2.2 million cars sold to American buyers, and the full-size lineup accounted for nearly 1.5 million units. The Caprice was a highly desirable model, with 181,000 orders. The Super Sport was also a separate series with coupe and convertible body styles, representing 119,300 orders.
The engine lineup available for the 1966 model year was impressive, to say the least. The L35 396 continued to be offered with 325 horsepower, but this time, buyers who wanted more power could order a 427 big-block engine with 390 horsepower. This was the L36 and carried an extra price tag of $181.
The top engine that could be installed on the Impala was the famous L72, which made its way to only $1,858 cars. It produced 425 horsepower but could be had for $312.
Photo: eBay seller tolu-988 This Impala comes with a 396, but it’s no longer under the hood. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but it’s unclear if this is the original factory engine.
The owner explains in the eBay post that the car is no longer original, so my recommendation if you’re specifically interested in this part is to call the seller and discuss the rest of the details. Sure, nothing beats a live inspection, but a walkaround video would also come in very handy.
The photos suggest this Impala has been sitting for quite some time, and the dirty interior confirms this is likely the case. The cabin looks good though, and despite being dirty and needing thorough cleaning, it looks to be in decent shape. No big parts appear to be missing, and that’s good news for someone who plans a complete restoration.
Photo: eBay seller tolu-988 The Impala requires rust repairs, but despite the obvious problems that you can see in the photos, it still has a clean frame. You will need a good restoration guy to fix everything on this Impala, but considering you’ll also get lots of extra parts, there’s a chance that putting the car back together and giving it a second chance won’t require as much effort as it looks at first glance.
Restoring a 1966 Impala can be worth the time and money if you’re specifically planning to sell it for profit, though I think the biggest shortcoming of this specimen is the non-SS setup. Collectors would pay big bucks for a 1966 Impala SS, especially with a 427 under the hood or sold separately (if original).
This doesn’t mean this non-SS doesn’t deserve our attention. It does, and there’s no doubt it would make an excellent showstopper if restored correctly.
Photo: eBay seller tolu-988 It’ll certainly be interesting to keep tabs on the last few minutes of this auction. First, this is a no-reserve auction, so the highest bidder will take it home when the battle ends. Second, nobody has submitted an offer so far, but this isn’t necessarily a surprise, as many potential buyers are waiting for the final seconds specifically to avoid the fierce competition that typically emerges during a no-reserve auction.
The Impala costs at least $5,000 - unless someone submits a higher offer - and the auction will end in just a few hours. The car is parked in Anoka, Minnesota, and will also require transportation, considering it doesn’t move on its own. Just make sure you have enough space to also get the engine and the extras included in the sale.
Via // eBay

Reborn Lancia Fulvia HF Gives the Ailing Italian Brand a True Hero Vehicle, Though Only Virtually
8 photos
Photo: mike.g.concepts / Instagram
Unfortunately for Lancia, 2025 wasn’t the year of rebirth that was heralded for the ailing Italian brand, with the relaunch going anything but as it was planned. As it turns out, having just one overpriced supermini in the lineup isn’t enough to conquer Europe once again – duh!
The historic Italian brand introduced the latest iteration of the Ypsilon supermini in early 2024, their first brand-new model even though it continued a nameplate for almost a decade and a half. Alas, the relaunch of the storied brand in export markets didn’t have an impact on the already-dwindling sales, and neither did the new model: Lancia sold less than 12k units in 2025, down 64% compared to the year before.
Stellantis isn’t abandoning the historic marque, luckily, especially since they spent quite a lot of money to return to France, Spain, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Germany. However, most likely nobody was fooled by the expensive fourth-generation Ypsilon, especially since there are other Stellantis options at lower costs, like the Peugeot 208 and Opel Corsa made using the same underpinnings.
Anyways, Stellantis kicked back into gear with ‘FastLane 2030,’ its new strategy back in May, and morphed Lancia alongside DS Automobiles into specialty brands under the leadership of Fiat and Citroen, respectively. Additionally, the company was on point at the 2026 Paris Motor Show with its second revival model, bringing back to life the storied Gamma – though not as a sedan anymore, and instead making it a premium compact crossover SUV.
The new fastback-style model is related to the DS No. 7 and 8 vehicles from DS Automobiles, as they all share the new STLA Medium architecture, and has all the latest technologies from the company, along with a hybrid option and no less than three all-electric powertrains packing up to 375 horsepower for the top tier or a range of up to 740 km (460 miles) for the middle EV model.
The flagship version is the all-electric Lancia Gamma HF Integrale, thus bringing back to life both the iconic HF and Integrale monikers, which became famous back in the day during Lancia’s age for both passenger cars and motorsport. Obviously, this makes people continue to dream about what could happen if Lancia finally takes flight once again, including the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.
For example, Mike G., the leader of the ' mike.g.concepts ' design studio, "fueled by adrenaline and innovation," has decided to bring back to CGI life another historic Lancia nameplate. He’s focusing on the Fulvia (Tipo 818), a model produced by Lancia between 1963 and 1976 with a name inspired by the Via Fulvia, a Roman road leading from Tortona to Turin.
Over the years, the real Lancia Fulvia played a key role in the company’s motorsport history and won the 1972 edition of the International Rally Championship, but also saw sales success with its three body styles: Berlina (four-door sedan), Coupe, and fastback coupe. Now, the pixel master has decided to reimagine the Lancia Fulvia as a hero model, a modern GT that uses the Fulvia HF moniker and blends the nameplate’s “rally heritage with sleek, minimalist lines.”
The CGI expert even devises a new, modern design language for this model, more precisely “featuring an aerodynamic coupé roofline inspired by the 037 instead of the classic ‘turret cabin’.” It also has a “driver-focused cockpit that blends pure driving dynamics with advanced digital instruments” and mixes a gated manual transmission with Alcantara and discrete but present displays. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mike G. (@mike.g.concepts)

2028 Toyota 4Runner Gets a Mid-Cycle Refresh Inside and Outside, Though Only Across Imagination Land
21 photos
Photo: AutoYa / YouTube
It’s pretty hard to believe, but the average new car prices just hit the next record, reaching over $51k – according to the latest data from Kelley Blue Book, the average transaction price (ATP) for a new vehicle soared to $51,109 in October 2026, which is $649 more than September, with SUVs and pickup trucks pushing all the prices higher.
The larger vehicles, combined with rising MSRPs due to inflation (or greed) and fewer incentives, are making new cars increasingly harder to afford. Of course, some brands keep on selling them because of their reputation and the great mix of choice. One such brand is Toyota , part of the TMNA – Toyota Motor North America – division of the Japanese automaker.
It has a diverse and well-built lineup, although its vehicles aren’t the cheapest around, with a few exceptions like the base models in the Corolla series. But Toyota knows how to entice people with models like the all-new RAV4 or the continuously popular mid-size pickup truck Tacoma or its big assortment of adventure SUVs.
For example, if you want a pickup truck with a manual transmission in the US, the only choice is from TMNA – Toyota retains the six-speed manual tranny for the 2027 Tacoma mid-size pickup truck, making it the only one with three pedals. Recently, the company also revived the Scion brand name, and it’s bringing a tiny Kei truck to America.
As such, it’s no wonder that everyone keeps an eye on Toyota – including the rumor mill and the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators. For example, the good folks over at the " AutoYa " info channel on YouTube have unofficially imagined the CGI look of the facelifted 2028 Toyota 4Runner family-adventure SUV – which has been around in its sixth-generation guise since early 2024 as a 2025 model year.
The new iteration of the mid-size adventure SUV is twinned with the N400 Toyota Tacoma mid-size pickup truck and the J250 Toyota Land Cruiser (Prado), along with the premium Lexus GX, among others, on the modular TNGA-F body-on-frame platform and has 2.4-liter turbo and hybrid powertrains with up to 326 combined hp. It’s been selling extremely well, too, with almost 108k units after nine months, up more than 61% compared to 2025.
But the host of the channel believes that, nevertheless, Toyota might decide to bring to market a mid-cycle refreshed 4Runner for the 2028 model year sometime in 2027, with technical updates as well as minor exterior and interior styling updates.
He then passes the baton to their virtual artist, a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators, saying that “We have illustrated how the new 4x4 Toyota 4Runner facelift could look and compared it with the current pre-facelifted model.”
Using the Toyota 4Runner TRD Off-Road or TRD Pro models as the base, along with the i-Force Max hybrid version under the hood, they showed us the potential changes in their latest unofficial, hypothetical design project: at the front we have a larger grille and restyled, slimmer LED headlights and new daytime running lights plus a reworked bumper.
Around the back, we can see a hint of new graphics for the LED taillights, and inside there are a bit more changes: the central display for the infotainment system, along with the controls for the climate unit, have been united into a single vertical screen, completely changing the layout of the interface in that zone. Also, there are numerous new colors – both outside and inside. So, what do you think – yay or nay?

1981 Classic Yacht Monaco Is a Priceless Gem for Today’s Gentleman
27 photos
Photo: Y.CO
A small, but elegant pleasure craft, the fully-refitted and lovingly maintained Monaco carries the nostalgia of the golden era of Gentleman’s yachts through the decades. In a world where monster megayachts share the same billionaire’s playgrounds with wooden sailing yachts and vintage motor yachts, the understated elegance of Monaco might seem too discrete to be noticed, yet it hides the prestigious status of the Feadship Heritage Fleet membership.
The tale of the Monaco yacht’s origin has gained the aura of a Viking legend over the decades, simply because of prosaic weather conditions. It seems that in 1981, the winter weather was so extreme that workers at the Dutch Kaag shipyard, who were bringing this Feadship to life, had to skate their way to the yard – a fairytale picture of the Monaco yacht being born.
Originally named Arkan, the winter-born new yacht also marked the beginning of a new phase in the evolution of Feadship design. To this day, Feadship yachts from the years prior to the 1980s flaunt the famous fantail stern. Arkan looks different, because the signature style was already beginning to change in the early ‘80s. However, it kept the covered aft deck, designed to be fully enclosed in bad weather conditions.
Photo: Feadship Boasting a slim silhouette of just under 125 feet (38 meters) with a 24-foot (7.2 meters) beam, Monaco was the spitting image of a graceful Gentleman’s yacht, the type of yachts that became popular around the mid-20th century for their understated elegance and noble spirit. Today, Monaco is endearingly referred to as “a petit Feadship”, in stark contrast to the contemporary mammoths delivered by this builder specializing in 50-to-100 meters long superyachts.
Quickly approaching its half-a-century anniversary, Monaco’s number of owners can be counted on the fingers of one hand. It first changed hands in the early ‘90s, when it was renamed Matanthar. Later, in the 2000s, it was renamed Monaco, still its name to this day, even though it seems to have changed ownership one more time. Prior to it being sold last month, Monaco had been with its last owners for more than 15 years, and says it all.
Millionaires who choose to invest in classic yachts , knowing full well that this often means further costs related to ample refits and overall maintenance, tend to be loyal to these old vessels and appreciate them for longer, not because they’ve put so much money into them, but because they seem them as collectors’ items. And Feadship gives them an extra reason to do so: becoming a member of the exclusive Heritage Fleet Club.
Photo: Pendennis As one of the most prolific and successful yacht builders in history, Feadship still counts hundreds of classic yachts still in operation today. That is why it has established The Feadship Heritage Fleet as an association for the owners of registered classic Feadships. The number one criterion is a proven age of at least three decades, but each yacht must be carefully confirmed and registered to become part of this exclusive club.
It’s not a cheap privilege. Following a €250 entry fee, members must pay an annual tax of €150 for yachts under 24 meters, and €500 for those over 24 meters. Membership comes with symbolic perks such as an official certificate and a stainless steel FHF logo that can be attached to the yacht, but what seems to matter the most is the companionship of like-minded owners and the ability to share personal experiences, tips about maintenance, and so on.
The Heritage Fleet wasn’t established on a whim. A dedicated research committee was set up a decade ago, in 2016, to work on a comprehensive archive of classic Feadships. There’s no other luxury yacht builder in the world to have a similar archive and Heritage Fleet, which demonstrates once again the immense historic value of these Dutch vessels.
Photo: Y.CO This is all to say that a yacht like Monaco, despite its humble size by today’s standards, is literally owning a piece of certified history. Just as important, the new owner is getting a pleasure craft in excellent condition, plus the benefit of a proven track record on the charter market. Monaco had less than a handful of owners in 45 years, and each one cared enough to invest in significant refits.
The acclaimed Pendennis shipyard alone has completed three of this refits, each during a different yacht ownership. The first one was in 1994. The second one, in 2005, was a more complex project that included a new bow-thruster, new switchboards, and a new distribution system. Beyond the technical upgrades, the newly-renamed Monaco received a fresh paint job, new teak decks, and an updated galley.
2016 was the year of the most comprehensive refit to this day. That is when Monaco’s Caterpillar D348 main engines were rebuilt to bring them back to zero hours. New generators were installed, and a complete exterior repaint ensured that the old yacht regained its former sparkle. All engineering systems were extensively upgraded during that seven-month refit, leaving the 1981 Feadship as good as new.
Photo: Y.CO To this day, the configuration and interior styling of the 124-foot Monaco prove to be versatile and popular. It’s highly unusual for a yacht this size to have both the master suite and the VIP suite on the main deck. It’s almost like having two master suites, and this is particularly welcomed by families during extended vacations. The two other suites are located on the lower deck, bringing the total number of guests that can accommodated to eight.
According to Feadship, skipping a fifth cabin, even if there was enough space for it, meant that all the four suites are very spacious, especially for a yacht this size. Together with crew quarters for up to seven members, this layout offers the benefits of a much bigger yacht with the footprint of an agile, more flexible 124-footer.
Although extensively refitted in terms of technical systems, Monaco hasn’t changed its classic style too much over time – even its hull color is the same as the original. The most noticeable addition to its amenities is a swim platform complete with aft stairs – no charter yacht can do without these things, and Monaco even carried a hefty toybox throughout its charter years.
Photo: Feadship The ingenious original configuration also included a wider range of outdoor options than you’d typically expect from a yacht in this size category. Guests have access to a small sunpad area on top of the wheelhouse, an observation lounge on the foredeck, and a generous area dedicated to al-fresco dining.
The original Terence Disdale interior design was discretely refreshed over time, but not dramatically changed. Guests can still admire the classic glossy mahogany that shows up in all Gentleman’s yachts, the traditional nautical theme in shades of cream and navy, and the formal dining spaces with a somber elegance. To some, this classic aesthetic might look a bit dated, but its suites the member of a classic yacht Heritage Fleet.
Proof of its enduring design and legacy, Monaco changed hands in October 2026, after being with its recent owners for more than 15 years. The last known asking price doesn’t reflect its true value: €3,9 million ($4.3 million), but the Heritage Fleet membership does.

Chart of the Week: National Truckload Index – USA SONAR : NTI.USA
The National Truckload Index (NTI), which measures dry van spot rate movement across the U.S., jumped to its highest level since July in early November. The NTI rarely climbs this early ahead of the holidays. What’s driving the increase, and what does it mean for this year’s holiday shipping season?
Many may point to fuel as the reason for this unseasonal rise. However, while elevated fuel costs may help explain some of the year-over-year growth and the longer-term divergence between spot and rejection rates this fall, it is difficult to tie fuel cleanly to this recent spot market jump. The NTI includes fuel, yet diesel costs have fallen roughly 3.5% since late October while the NTI has risen more than 4% over the same period.
Fuel does influence rates with a lag, but diesel hasn’t seen a sharp increase since early September, which is well beyond the typical lag of a few weeks.
As mentioned in earlier articles , carriers can’t always pass along fuel costs unless the market will bear it. The same is true for any input cost, as many businesses know from trying to pass upstream inflation on to their customers. This latest jump appears to be driven by market conditions, though the picture is nuanced because there has been no corresponding rise in tender rejection rates.
National dry van rejection rates have been trending lower since July, though still elevated. Rejection rates above 10% is still a sign of insufficient capacity. Rejection rates and spot rates don’t move in a one-to-one relationship for several reasons, even if they tend to track each other over time. Perhaps the most important distinction is that tender data represents the much larger contracted freight market, while the spot market is a fringe environment that accounts for roughly 10% to 25% of truckload freight, depending on the market.
The recent disconnect between the contract and spot markets may be tied to a surge of freight moving outside of contracted agreements. On last week’s episode of Freightonomics , Dr. Zac Rogers, co-author of the Logistics Managers’ Index (LMI), said that many retailers appear to have waited until the last minute to bring inventory into the country.
This is reflected in the sharp jump in inventory level growth in the October LMI. The reading of 66.9 was the highest for this component of the index since 2022. The last-minute surge was the product of demand uncertainty, rising inventory holding costs, and more streamlined supply chains.
Demand uncertainty has been the story of 2026, as many retailers expected consumers to pull back on spending due to ongoing inflation. That has happened in some areas more than others, but in aggregate it has largely washed out.
Shippers have also been dealing with their own inflation, as the cost of holding inventory has increased significantly. This has pushed them toward just-in-time (JIT) ordering, which they have used with great success. With holding costs this high, the extra expense of shipping later is easier to justify. Intermodal has benefited greatly from elevated trucking and warehousing costs, growing by double digits over 2025 levels.
Dr. Rogers also noted that supply chains have evolved since COVID, becoming more streamlined and flexible. This lets shippers move freight through their networks more precisely, cutting transit time and allowing them to delay orders.
With the holidays approaching and the truckload market still not fully recovered, shippers likely know that waiting until the week before Thanksgiving will be expensive, so some are trying to get ahead of the curve.
Some of this freight may also be rail volume shifting back to truck after disruptions hit BNSF and CSX in recent weeks. Domestic container volumes still have not fully recovered and appear to be hitting a ceiling, unlike the previous two years, when domestic container volumes grew into December.
About the Chart of the Week
The FreightWaves Chart of the Week is a chart selection from SONAR that provides an interesting data point to describe the state of the freight markets. A chart is chosen from thousands of potential charts on SONAR to help participants visualize the freight market in real time. Each week a Market Expert will post a chart, along with commentary, live on the front page. After that, the Chart of the Week will be archived on FreightWaves.com for future reference.
SONAR aggregates data from hundreds of sources, presenting the data in charts and maps and providing commentary on what freight market experts want to know about the industry in real time.
The FreightWaves data science and product teams are releasing new datasets each week and enhancing the client experience.

1969 Dodge Charger R/T Becomes the World's Most Expensive Non-Hemi Model
17 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
Mecum's Las Vegas 2026 auction just came to a close, with 20 vehicles changing hands for six-figure sums. Most of them are high-profile classics, and one just set a new record. It's a 1969 Dodge Charger R/T that sold for $148,000.
Granted, this figure is not overly spectacular compared to the Charger Daytona or Hemi-powered rigs, but that's the thing: it doesn't have a high wing and it's not a Hemi. It was born with the standard 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, and it's the first of its kind to get that kind of money.
At nearly $150K, it's the most expensive non-Hemi 1969 Charger. Naturally, I'm also excluding restomods and movie cars from this list (the "General Lee" promo car sold for over $400,000 many years ago). It trumped the previous record, set in May 2026, by $33,000. And it also fetched nearly as much as some Hemi examples auctioned off in recent years.
So, what exactly prompted classic car enthusiasts to bid well over $100,000 for a very regular Charger R/T? Well, for starters, it's a very original Mopar. It has a numbers-matching drivetrain and crossed the block with loads of original documentation, including the broadcast sheet, window sticker, fender tag, and owner's manual. It also has air conditioning and front disc brakes, both of which are desirable features.
But I'm pretty sure that it also has a lot to do with the color combo. Yes, the EW1 White paint may seem mundane, but it's a relatively rare hue. The old 1969 Dodge Charger Registry, which hasn't been updated in a while, provides some useful info on that. Only 4% of the vehicles listed there were ordered in this color.
It's difficult to get an accurate statistic based on incomplete information, but it probably means that fewer than 800 R/Ts rolled off the assembly line with white paint . Then there's also the red interior. The ad says that this is a rare combo, and that's true because red is the rarest color when it comes to vinyl bucket-seat models.
Again, the 1969 Charger Registry comes in handy, revealing that only 3.7% of all vinyl interiors were ordered in this hue. If we factor in all upholstery types, red vinyl cars represent only 2.9% of the total production. As for the white-over-red combo, there's no official statistic, but probably fewer than 30 units were delivered like this.
If we also factor in the red bumblebee stripe and all the other options, this Charger may very well be a one-of-a-kind vehicle. Speaking of which, the window sticker shows 20 options, totaling $881, which is a 25% premium over the base price. The same document reveals that the car was built as a dealer demonstrator .
What's your take on this R/T? Is it worth nearly $150K, or is it way too expensive for a non-Hemi Mopar? Let me know in the comments section below.

'The Gentleman’s Racer' 1967 Pontiac GTO Would Be Capable of Taking on a Green Hell If It Were Real
6 photos
Photo: wnvld / Instagram
Ringbrothers, probably one of the best-known American custom car builders and aftermarket parts manufacturers, established and operated by the brothers Jim and Mike Ring out of Spring Green, Wisconsin, has done it again – they mesmerized the 2026 SEMA Show once again.
This year they have done it with Billie, aka the Billy Goat , a 650-horsepower Pontiac ‘GTO.’ As per tradition, Ringbrothers is classically associated with the SEMA Show in Las Vegas, Nevada, where they often unveil the radical custom creations – which are also incredibly rare to begin with.
So, this year at the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) Show in Las Vegas, the star of the red carpet was Billie, another cool name like Octavia (a restomod 1971 Aston Martin DBS with an 800-hp Ford Coyote V8), Kingpin (a 1969 Ford Mustang Mach 1 drenched in carbon fiber and 3D-printed parts), Recoil, the 1964 Chevrolet Chevelle, or Defiant, a heavily modded 1972 AMC Javelin AMX.
The year’s headliner was a custom-built 1965 Pontiac that was painstakingly recreated as a GTO over more than 5,500 hours of work from an old Pontiac Tempest Convertible that became a 650-hp GOAT (Greatest of All Time) with a five-inch-wider body and a ton of handcrafted stuff all over the place. Naturally, this inevitably gave people ideas – or dreams, in the case of the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.
More precisely, Andreas Wennevold, the virtual artist behind the ' wnvld ' account on social media, has a knack for American muscle in vintage-modern form, as it turns out, and his latest unofficial, hypothetical design project is “The Gentleman’s Racer,” a follow-up to the Ringbrothers Billie “designed to handle the Green Hell.”
This 1967 Pontiac GTO is the product of a wacky idea, as the pixel master firmly believes “there’s just something really cool about a track-capable big-body muscle car” from America. His digital concept reinterprets the first-generation Pontiac GTO, although the second iteration is arguably even more famous than all the others, and gives it a longtail restomod treatment focused on achieving greatness at the local racetrack instead of the countless custom car shows around America.
The virtual GTO is clearly inspired by Billie from Ringbrothers at least in terms of paint, but it comes with performance-focused design elements like the new carbon fiber aero front spoiler, the central windshield wiper, the side A-pillar air holes, the yellow-letter Goodyear race tires, and Y-spoke forged alloy wheels with red brake calipers tucked behind them.
We also couldn’t help but notice the new LED headlights and the big LED taillights, the extended fender flares that make it a widebody, and combine with the rest of the carbon fiber aerodynamic package, which includes wild and wide door steps and a humongous diffuser attached to that extra-long rear. Inside, although there’s no direct cockpit POV, we can still make out the competition-grade bucket seats and the full roll cage. Next-Gen 2028 Toyota Corolla Imagined Inside and Out, Is It an Upgrade or a Downgrade?
12 photos
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | AutoYa Interior
The world’s best-selling car ever, with over 50 million units sold worldwide ever since it first broke cover back in 1966, the Toyota Corolla , is getting a major redesign, and we are not talking about a mere mid-cycle refresh, but an entirely new generation, set to replace the current one.
Speaking of the latter, the E210 Toyota Corolla is in the twelfth generation, as you likely know, and given that it has been around since 2018 for the hatchback and 2019 for the sedan/estate, with a facelift introduced for the 2023 model year, it is an aging product. And while traditional passenger cars are not that popular anymore, especially in Western markets, this model won’t be put to sleep, and it also won’t turn into a crossover of some sort for the next generation.
After all, that’s what the Toyota Corolla Cross is for, because this model is a thing, in case you forgot, and has been one since mid-2020, which is when it hit the assembly line. It is made in Japan, Thailand, Taiwan, Malaysia, China, Pakistan, South Africa, Brazil, and the United States, and as you already know, it is based on the TNGA-C platform. Thus, it shares its construction not only with the E210 Corolla, but also with the Prius, C-HR, Lexus UX, and many other models.
As for the traditional model, namely the regular Corolla, it comes to life in the United States, at the Blue Springs factory in Mississippi, as well as in the United Kingdom, Turkey, Brazil, China, Taiwan, Thailand, and Japan. The compact car has been offered over the years with a plethora of gasoline engines, as well as several hybrids, and the powertrain family obviously varies from one market to the other.
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | AutoYa Interior Now, Toyota is about to retire the current generation , introducing it with a new one, which is expected to come out in 2027, likely as a 2028 model year. Word on the street is that the next-generation Toyota Corolla could be offered as a liftback, thus morphing the lines between a traditional sedan and a hatchback, and it should feature gasoline, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and even electric assembly, for a very versatile powertrain family.
The future model was apparently teased a few months ago, with the picture suggesting that it will look similar to the Toyota Corolla Concept presented at the Japan Mobility Show in 2025. And as we already told you, it might come out as a liftback, and this could be the only body style available. It should be based on an updated version of the TNGA-C construction, so while it may look new inside and out, it will utilize familiar underpinnings.
Power-wise, the self-charging hybrid could be a new 1.5-liter four-pot, with an alleged combined output of 134 horsepower, perhaps with an optional all-wheel drive system. A plug-in hybrid will presumably offer a beefier electric motor and a bigger battery pack, and an EV is supposedly in the works, too, perhaps with a an optional dual-motor setup sitting at the top of the range. The regular one might get a turbo’d 1.5- or a 2.0-liter mill, and the GR Corolla will live on, allegedly with a 2L four-banger making around 400 hp.
Over the last few months, we have seen a few rendering takes on the next-generation Toyota Corolla, and while it is still hard to imagine that the new one will look similar, or perhaps identical, depending on whom you ask, they were mostly based on the Toyota Corolla Concept from 2025, mentioned above.
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | AutoYa Interior That study barely resembles a Corolla. It was styled by the brand’s European design center in Nice, France, and looks like something that has come from the future. Toyota’s hammerhead lights, full-width taillights, a narrow lower air intake in the front bumper, a subtle vent at the base of the windshield, and quirky styling cues define its exterior design. And the show car has been used once again as a blank canvas for the digital illustrations shared in the gallery.
Signed by AutoYa Interior and released on YouTube earlier this week in the form of a CGI-infused video, the project in question has been imagined from several angles on the outside, and looks pretty much like the Toyota Corolla Concept. The rendering artist has sketched it out in several paint finishes, and has gone as far as illustrating the interior, too, again, in quite a few colors.
The cockpit reminds us of the old Toyota Prius , to some extent. It is a screen-filled cabin with the central infotainment screen and a passenger display sitting behind a single pane of glass, from what we can see, and a third display mounted behind the steering wheel, and neatly integrated into the dashboard panel. The center console is definitely on the quirky side of things, but the steering wheel looks quite traditional.
Now, there is no clear indication that the next-gen Toyota Corolla will look anything like this, but if it does, would you buy it? And better yet, do you considered this rendered project an upgrade or a downgrade from the outgoing Corolla?

The 6 Slowest Lamborghinis Ever Built Are Also Some of the Coolest
28 photos
Photo: Lamborghini
There are a few car brands out there that started out from a vengeance, and Lamborghini is probably the best known in that category. To be more precise, Lamborghini only exists as a supercar maker because of an argument about a fast car that didn’t even wear a Racing Bull badge.
Unless you’ve been living under a rock for your entire life or simply have had no interest whatsoever in automotive trivia, the story of how the Sant’Agata Bolognese brand was founded is one of the most common pieces of Italian supercar lore.
To refresh your memory, the story goes that Ferrucio Lamborghini, who was a wealthy tractor manufacturer, constantly complained to Enzo Ferrari about the poor quality of the clutches in the Ferraris he owned. Severely irritated, Enzo allegedly told Ferruccio to stick to tractors. Instead, Lamborghini started his own car company in 1963.
Three years later, Lamborghini Automobili unleashed the Miura, the mid-engine V12 that more or less invented the modern supercar. Then came the incredible Countach, the Diablo, the Murcielago, Aventador, and recently the Revuelto. With a few exceptions, mostly because of regulations, each of them has been wider, louder, and always faster than its predecessor.
These are the Lamborghinis of bedroom posters, but they aren’t the only cars that made the company what it is today. You see, for the better part of its first three decades of existence, Lamborghini was small potatoes far from what it represents now, as it was always short of money and regularly close to collapse.
Its ownership changed hands several times, with Ferruccio himself selling his majority stake in 1972 and leaving the automotive industry altogether in 1974. The company he left even went bankrupt at the end of 1978. Obviously, with all these conundrums happening constantly, a company couldn’t pull through on selling V12 flagships alone.
To survive, Lamborghini eventually needed to make less expensive cars as well, or cars that suit the tax or emissions rules in certain markets, and sometimes even cars that make sense to almost no one outside Sant’Agata Bolognese.
As it happens, some of those “other Lamborghinis” were slow, albeit not in the traditional “0 to 60 in eventually” slow. They were definitely sluggish in the context of having the same badge as a 200-mph, mid-engine V12 Lambo, though. Don’t get me wrong, a Lamborghini that takes more than 7 seconds to reach 100 kph (62 mph), or begins to run out of breath short of reaching 250 kph (155 mph) doesn’t seem so deserving of the Raging Bull badge, yet a few of them have existed.
In other words, just like with other similar carmakers, like Ferrari, not everything that came out wearing a Lambo badge has been the fastest thing on four wheels during its era. On top of it, not all “slow” Lamborghinis have been entry level models either. The following shortlist of “lethargic Lambos" comprises all sorts of cars, from V12-powered grand tourers to V8 baby Lambos and there is even a V12 off-roader originally made for the military.
Lamborghini 400 GT 2+2: The Gentleman’s Private Express Train, Upstaged at its Own Debut The 400 GT in 2+2 guise had the bad luck of being introduced to the world at the 1966 Geneva Motor Show, which was the same venue where Lamborghini also unveiled the Miura P400. This was definitely a planned but terrible coincidence, because one was a mid-engined sensation that changed how fast cars should be made and the other was essentially a taller 350 GT with two extra seats.
Proportionally, the majority of people praised the Miura over the 400 GT 2+2, but it’s the front-engined V12 that Ferrucio actually wanted to build all along. Despite how the most successful Lambos ever ended up being like, he was more of a fan of reasonably fast, quiet, and comfortable grand tourers.
Photo: RM Sotheby's The 400 GT 2+2 did tick a lot of boxes in its segment. Its Bizzarrini-designed V12 was enlarged to 3.9 liters compared to its predecessor and developed 320 PS (316 HP) and 374 Nm (276 lb-ft) of torque, fed by no less than six twin-choke Weber carburetors. Lamborghini also replaced the earlier ZF gearbox with a five-speed of its own design, while also adding a limited-slip differential.
Despite room for two (small) passengers), the wheelbase was identical with the 350 GT, with the two extra seats being carved out of the existing cabin by slightly raising the roofline and reshaping the floor. That said, it was slightly heavier than its predecessors, which made it a bit slower.
With a 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration time of around 7.5 seconds and a top speed of around 250 kph (155 mph), the 400 GT 2+2 was no slouch for the era, but in the context of the Miura sharing its stage it felt like a snail. In other words, the long-hooded grand tourer belongs on this list more as a marker than an actual culprit, but it was still the slowest Lamborghini of its day.
Lamborghini Islero and Espada: Ferruccio’s Favorites, Yet the Ones Nobody Took to the Autostrada Named after the bull that killed famous matador Manolete, the Islero is arguably the second-fiercest name for a Lamborghini after the Diablo. It arrived at the 1968 Geneva Motor Show as a replacement for the 400 GT 2+2, where it shared the stand with the Espada, which was named after the sword used by matadors to kill the bull.
Like its predecessor, which was upstaged by the Miura, the Islero caught almost no one’s attention compared to the Espada, which was a true four-seater that looked a lot more dramatic. One reason could have been that the more traditional-looking (apart from its funky popup headlights) Islero had been designed by Mario Marazzi, while the Espada was the work of legendary Marcello Gandini. The Espada also broke a lot of norms regarding the exterior design of a grand tourer.
Photo: Lamborghini Both cars were powered by the same Bizzarrini V12, which sent a similar amount of power as their 400 GT 2+2 predecessors to the rear wheels through a Lamborghini-designed 5-speed manual transmission. The Espada was larger and much heavier, closer to an American-style grand tourer, and it also offered a 3-speed automatic transmission as an option.
With no update regarding their outputs and increased weight, both the Islero but especially the Jarama were not exactly quicker, nor faster than the cars they replaced, making for a pretty peculiar Lamborghini duo. A year later, Lamborghini did introduce the Islero S, which came with 350 horsepower, bigger brakes and a revised rear suspension, also increasing its top speed to about 260 kph (161 mph), while the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) time dropped to 6.2 seconds.
Those numbers didn’t help much, as the Islero only lasted for about 14 months as part of the lineup, leaving everyone except Ferruccio underwhelmed. It is said that the company’s founder used one as his personal car, as did his brother Edmondo, but overall it was too discreet in both sales and performance, and the Espada wasn’t much of an improvement in that regard either.
Lamborghini Jarama 400 GT: More Power, More Weight, But No More Speed The Jarama was Lamborghini’s third attempt at the same idea in about five years. Like the 400 GT 2+@ and the Islero before it, it was a front-engined V12 coupe with two small rear seats. The somewhat unusual explanation for its existence in the first place was that the Islero would have needed a major redesign to meet new American safety and emission rules, so Lamborghini simply decided to start from scratch.
Well, almost from scratch since the Jarama was actually based on a shortened version of the Espada platform, with which it shared its engine and transmission(s). Presented at the Geneva Motor Show in 1970, it was designed by long-time collaborator Marcello Gandini. Gandini gave it a wide, somewhat blunt-looking and angular body, with half-exposed headlights, which was a very different and more flamboyant look compared to the more restrained and traditional-looking Islero.
Photo: RM Sotheby's The Jarama’s wheelbase was not only shorter than the Espada’s but it was even smaller than that of the Islero, making for the most compact 2+2 in Lamborghini’s lineup. Despite the coincidence, its name wasn’t a tribute to the Spanish racing circuit but actually referred to the Jarama region in Spain, known for breeding fighting bulls.
Its engine was the familiar Bizzarrini design V12 with 6 Weber carburettors, albeit it was now rated at 350 horsepower and a healthy 392 Nm (289 lb-ft) of torque. While being 30 horsepower more powerful than the Islero, the smaller Jarama was actually about 150 kg (330 pounds) heavier. In other words, the extra power and the extra mass pretty much cancelled each other out, with its top speed revolving around the 245 kph (161 mph) mark, while the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration took over 7 seconds.
Despite, once again, being one of Ferruccio’s favorites, with a later-model Jarama S S being once again his personal car, not many other people shared this view. In fact, almost everyone thought it was too slow, especially for a Lamborghini, and in some ways you could say they were right.
Lamborghini Urraco P111: The Baby Lamborghini That Arrived in the U.S. Short of 40 Horsepower The Urraco was supposed to be the car that would transform Lamborghini from a boutique to a volume sports carmaker. It was a compact 2+2 with a mid-mounted V8, and it was once again styled by Marcello Gandini at Bertone. The model was aimed to disturb the party held by cars like the Porsche 911, Ferrari Dino, or the Maserati Merak.
Shown at the Turin Motor Show in 1970, it took another two years for production to begin and first customers didn’t get their cars until 1973, by which time the oil crisis was in full swing and Lamborghini was slowly sliding toward bankruptcy. From the start, the U.S. was supposed to be the Urraco's biggest market, but getting there meant meeting federal safety and emission laws.
Photo: RM Sotheby's To prepare it, Lamborghini swapped its Weber carburetors for Solex units and bolted on those dreadful-looking impact bumpers, completely changing both its specs and its looks for the worse. Power for the 2.5-liter V8 used fell from 220 PS (217 HP) to around 180 PS (177 HP), which was even less than the 2.0-liter Urraco P200 that Lamborghini sold at home to get around Italy’s 38 percent tax on engines larger than 2.0 liters.
The European Urraco P250 was good for 240 kph (149 mph), with 100 kph (62 mph) coming up in 6.9 seconds. The American-only P111 barely managed 215 kph (134 mph), while the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) took almost 10 seconds.
It was simply the slowest Lamborghini ever produced up to that point, and with an exterior look that only a mother would love, it's no wonder that only 21 units were ever built and sold. To put things into perspective, a Corvette Stingray 454 from 1974 would hit 100 kph (62 mph) in under 6 seconds, making it almost twice as quick as the twice as expensive baby Lambo.
Lamborghini LM002: By Far, the Slowest V12 Lamborghini Ever Each of the cars on this list were slow mainly because they had too little power for the Lamborghini badge, especially when it comes to the Urraco P111. On the other hand, the LM002 had 450 horsepower, which is obviously more than anything else, and by a wide margin.
In short, its lackluster on-road performance was obviously not for a lack of power, but for weighing about 2,700 kg (5,952 pounds) and having the drag coefficient of a small building. The “Rambo Lambo,” as it was affectionately nicknamed, had started as a military project, with Lamborghini building a prototype called the Cheetah.
While the original was powered by a rear-mounted Chrysler V8, the next two versions were upgraded to a front-mounted Lamborghini V12, or exactly the same engine used in the Countach, to be more precise.
Photo: Lamborghini The name LM002 came from “Lamborghini Militaria, second prototype,” although it was the third if we also take into account the Cheetah. The civilian production version was unveiled at the Brussels Motor Show in 1986, and its specifications list sounded a bit like a dream. The 5.2-liter V12 developed 450 horsepower and 500 Nm (369 lb-ft) of torque, sent to all four wheels through a 5-speed manual and a two-speed transfer case.
In short, it was the most powerful and arguably the most brutal-looking off-roader on the planet. Its tires were developed by Pirelli specifically for the LM002 and used run-flat technology. As you would expect, fuel consumption was not its strong point, with 30 to 35 liters per 100 km (7 to 8 mpg US) being common, which is probably why Lamborghini fitted it with a 169-liter (45 gallons) fuel tank.
Then again, nobody bought a Lamborghini expecting it to sip fuel like a family car, but its on-road performance was not exactly stellar either. As a matter of fact, it is by far the slowest road-going Lamborghini in history, and its record will probably never be beaten.
While it was quicker than an Urraco from 0 to 100 kph (62 mph), the LM002’s weight and brick-shaped aerodynamics gave it a top speed of just 210 kph (130 mph). On the other hand, it’s also the only production Lamborghini that could climb 120-degree gradients, thus also making it the quickest thoroughbred off-roader of its time.

Chicago Dealer Selling 2025 Chevy Corvette Z06 With 7,000 Miles, What’s Your Take on the Price?
12 photos
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago
The Z06 may no longer be the best track-focused version of the C8-generation Chevrolet Corvette, as the lineup is now vaster than ever and includes some truly mind-blowing models, but it remains a great machine, and it is still a lot of car for the money.
In today’s bowtie brand’s ‘Vette family, the Z06 slots between the Grand Sport X and the ZR1 in terms of pricing, as it kicks off at $121,800, excluding destination, options, and dealer fees. For the Grand Sport X, you will have to fork out at least $110,000, and the regular Grand Sport starts at $86,300. As for the base Stingray, it has an MSRP of $71,300 attached to it. The ZR1 and ZR1X can be ordered from $198,300 and $227,800.
These two offer insane performance that is more comparable to modern-day hypercars rather than regular supercars, and one must be extremely lucky if they land an example for only a little over the MSRP. That’s because these things tend to command huge markups, as you likely already know. As for the Z06 , it usually goes for more down-to-earth sums, and the entry-level can actually be had for very close to the MSRP, whereas superior grades can easily exceed $160,000.
A used 2025 model year Z06 version of the C8 Chevrolet Corvette can drop to under $100,000, and trade-in values can reach $80,000. However, realistically speaking, you will still have to fork out a six-digit sum for a nice example, and sometimes over $130,000 and $140,000 for a low-mileage car in a range-topping configuration that packs plenty of gear. To no one’s surprise, cars with in the 2LZ and 3LZ specs with the Z07 pack are obviously worth more than the base 1LZ trim level.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago But why mention this particular model year in the above paragraph? Because the Chevrolet Corvette Z06 pictured above is a 2025 model year car. It is presented in a glossy dark blue shade with several black accents on the outside, and rides on black wheels wrapped in sticky tires from Michelin. The alloys spin around the silver brake calipers with white branding, and everything looks OEM to us, including the wing that rests on the rear deck.
The paint looks perfect in the images that the selling dealer recently shared on social media, and we can only see a tiny bit of wear on the driver’s seat outer bolster. This machine features black leather upholstery stitched together with yellow double string for contrast on certain elements, has a flat-bottom steering wheel, a black headliner, yellow seatbelts, the usual carbon fiber trim, the wall of buttons, and the dual-screen setup, among other things.
As for why it looks almost new, we mentioned it in the title, and it is the mileage. This particular Chevrolet Corvette Z06 has only 7,000 miles (~11,300 km) or so under its belt, so it hasn’t seen a huge amount of driving, as that’s pretty much normal mileage. The vendor hasn’t revealed much about it, other than the exterior and interior colors, mileage, model year, and asking price, and we will reveal the latter toward the end of this story.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago Before we do that, we will remind you that the Z06 version of the C8 Chevy Corvette comes with a flat-plane crank V8 engine developed with Ferrari’s indirect know-how. The mill has a 5.5-liter displacement, and produces 670 horsepower with no outside intervention. That’s 680 horsepower for the metric crowd, and 500 kilowatts. The official thrust is rated at 460 pound-feet (624 Nm), in case you forgot.
Yeah, the output and thrust may be nothing compared to the ZR1 and ZR1X versions of the model, but that is still more than enough for daily drives. With the Z07 Performance Package, the vehicle will reach 60 mph (97 kph) in a neck-snapping 2.6 seconds. And that’s similar to the Lamborghini Temerario, a machine that costs roughly three times as more, and packs a lot more grunt from its plug-in hybrid V8. The quarter mile takes 10.6 seconds, the spec sheet shows, with an exit speed of 131 mph (211 kph).
The dealer, which is known as @motorcarsofchicago on Instagram, offers finances, accepts trade-ins, and hates direct messages, as the social media post embedded below reveals. But how much does this 2025 Chevrolet Corvette Z06 cost? Well, unless you said $132,995, then you are wrong, because this was the asking price of the track-focused blue-collar supercar at the time of writing.
In my opinion, that’s a decent asking price for this thing in today’s used car market, but you can feel free to contradict me in the comments section below. And while you’re at it, tell us whether you would really blow $133K on a normal mileage Z06 from the 2025 model year, assuming that you were indeed shopping for such a thing.
